title: Low-carbon concrete of the Pinglu Canal: key challenges and solutions
abstract: Abstract As a key component of the New Western Land-Sea Corridor in China, the high-quality construction of the Pinglu Canal holds considerable significance. Concrete, the most widely used construction material in the project, presents several distinctive engineering characteristics, including large-scale applications over long spans, complex structures for water-saving ship locks, stringent durability requirements, tight construction schedules, and constrained working spaces. These factors not only create technical challenges but also pose a severe, systemic low-carbon challenge due to the huge carbon emission baseline and high carbon intensity associated with concrete construction. This study analyzes the key challenges for concrete engineering in the Pinglu Canal, and proposes a framework for solutions that integrates structural safety with low-carbon synergy across multiple stages and multiple levels. Based on this framework, this study further summarizes the demonstration solutions already implemented in the Pinglu Canal. Drawing from the Pinglu Canal case, this study aims to provide theoretical references and practical guidance for the low-carbon construction of modern canal engineering projects.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The Pinglu Canal, with a total length of 134.2 km and a designed annual one-way throughput capacity of 89 million tonnes, starts at the Pingtang River Estuary in the city of Nanning and ends at Qinzhou Port, providing access to the Beibu Gulf. As an important part of the New Western Land-Sea Corridor, the canal connects major inland cities in southwestern China with coastal cities in Guangxi. Upon completion, it will provide the shortest and most economical sea outlet for southwestern China.

Construction of the Pinglu Canal officially began in August 2022, and the substantial completion is scheduled for the end of September 2026. While its primary function is navigation, the canal is also designed to integrate multiple purposes, including water supply, irrigation, and flood control [ 1 ]. The canal system comprises three inland waterway hubs arranged from upstream to downstream: Madao, Qishi, and Qingnian. To achieve efficient utilization of water resources, the Madao and Qishi hubs are equipped with water-saving locks that employ a three-tier, stacked water-saving basin design, whereas the Qingnian hub adopts a mutual filling-and-emptying water-saving method. The canal has a 100-year design life, which imposes extremely high requirements on durability of its construction materials.

Concrete is the foundational material used in the Pinglu Canal, with the largest material consumption and the most significant carbon footprint. The total pouring volume of concrete for the canal’s work is approximately 11.9 million m 3 , covering hub projects, waterway engineering, bridges, supporting buildings, and other ancillary works. Among these components, the concrete volume for the three key hubs reaches 5.846 million m 3 . As the primary source of carbon emissions, concrete works have become critical to achieving the canal’s low-carbon goals, making it imperative to integrate low-carbon principles throughout the design, construction, and maintenance stages of concrete engineering [ 2 ]. Overall, safe, durable, and low-carbon concrete engineering constitutes the core technical foundation for ensuring the Pinglu Canal’s 100-year service life and achieving its low-carbon goals.

sections.heading: Long linear project
paragraphs: Unlike conventional concrete projects, the Pinglu Canal project is characterized by its exceptionally long, linear layout. The Pinglu Canal extends 134.2 km across varied terrains, and the total volume of concrete works is approximately 3.5 times that of the Hoover Dam in the United States [ 3 ]. The long-span, linear nature of the project creates substantial management challenges. Construction of the hubs and waterways is divided into 15 sections, making material transportation and site organization difficult. In addition, the large volume of concrete under such a long-span also results in a huge carbon emission baseline, leading to serious challenges for carbon emission control.

Moreover, construction of the Pinglu Canal involves extensive demolition works along its route, including bridges, houses, hydraulic facilities, and temporary facilities, which will generate a large amount of solid waste. Specifically, 22 bridges need to be demolished, producing approximately 180 000 m 3  of waste concrete [ 4 ]. Earthwork excavation for the Pinglu Canal is expected to reach approximately 300 million m 3 , involving 23 types of geotechnical materials with complex compositions and scattered distribution [ 1 ]. It can be seen that the solid waste from the Pinglu Canal’s construction is large in quantity, while also offering considerable potential for carbon emission reduction.

sections.heading: Mass concrete for water-saving ship locks
paragraphs: In the Pinglu Canal, 90% of the concrete used in the hub projects is mass concrete. Due to its large volume, the heat generated by cement hydration within mass concrete is difficult to dissipate in time, making it highly susceptible to thermal cracking and thereby threatening structural safety. Moreover, different from conventional mass-concrete structures, water-saving ship locks are adopted in the Madao Hub and Qishi Hub. Compared with non-water-saving ship locks, the water-saving ship locks require an additional 32 water delivery valves, 24 hydraulic hoists, and 8 working valves, as well as a water delivery system consists of 4 sections, 8 branch culverts, and 96 sets of water delivery branch openings. This results in a large number of reserved openings, embedded components, and construction joints, along with high precision requirements. In addition, the existence of water-saving basins increases the overall construction quantities. The Pinglu Canal innovatively adopts a three-tier, stacked layout for the water-saving basins (Fig.  1  [ 5 ]), which nonetheless results in an increase of approximately 500 000 m 3  in concrete volume and about 10 million m 3  in earthwork excavation compared to a lock of the same scale, thereby raising carbon emissions. Fig. 1 Layout plan of Madao hub

Meanwhile, the area along the Pinglu Canal is mainly characterized by a subtropical monsoon climate, with long and hot summers. The average daily maximum temperature ranges 32–35 ℃ in summer, and remains above 20 °C in spring and autumn. Such high temperatures make it difficult to control the hydration heat of mass concrete, requiring temperature control measures at every stage, including mixing, transportation, and pouring, which significantly increases energy consumption.

In summary, the use of mass concrete in water-saving ship locks demands more stringent construction standards and results in a larger project scale. Combined with the hot climate, these factors together pose significant challenges for carbon emission control.

sections.heading: Long-term durability
paragraphs: Connecting the Beibu Gulf and the Qinjiang River, the canal is subject to seawater intrusion, with transports chloride ions upstream into inland waters. Chloride ions damage the passive membrane of the reinforcement, causing corrosion and expansive cracking. These cracks then accelerate the penetration of chloride ions and moisture, creating a “vicious cycle” that results in concrete spalling, rebar exposure, and a severe loss of load-bearing capacity [ 6 ]. Furthermore, the hot and humid climate along the Pinglu Canal promotes erosion, leading to high pore saturation within concrete and accelerated chemical reaction rates. These factors greatly increase the corrosion rate of the steel reinforcement and pose a severe challenge to the durability of concrete structures.

Moreover, to facilitate efficient navigation, rapid filling and emptying of water are required. Combined with rapid gate operation, this process generates high-velocity, alternating flows between the culverts and water-saving basins. The concrete is easily affected by abrasion from sediment-laden water and by cavitation erosion [ 7 ], especially at bends and flow-diversion zones, where concrete surface deterioration can significantly reduce durability. Furthermore, structures such as mooring dolphins, which serve as key components for vessel berthing and energy dissipation, are frequently subjected to impacts and friction, posing further challenges to durability. To achieve the century-long service life goal of the project, the canal concrete must also exhibit good impermeability, crack resistance, and resistance to wetting-drying cycles.

The durability of concrete structures directly influences the maintenance intervals and frequency of an engineering project. Insufficient durability leads to frequent maintenance, which increases carbon emissions and life-cycle carbon burden. Moreover, large-scale maintenance activities may interrupt navigation, severely affecting the operational efficiency and economic performance of the Pinglu Canal. Therefore, the Pinglu Canal project should be designed to achieve a 100-year service life without requiring major repairs, thereby minimizing navigation interruptions and additional carbon emissions caused by maintenance.

sections.heading: Rapid construction
paragraphs: The planned construction period for the Pinglu Canal is 52 months. Within this limited time period, large-scale concrete works including navigation channel works, hub structures, bridges, and ancillary buildings, must be completed, requiring the placement of approximately 11.9 million m 3  of concrete. For comparison, the Three Gorges Project involved a total concrete volume of approximately 28 million m 3 , with construction starting in 1994 and the main structure completed in 2009 [ 8 ], corresponding to an average annual placement rate of around 1.8 million m 3 . In contrast, the Pinglu Canal requires an average annual placement rate of 2.7 million m 3 —approximately 50% higher than that of the Three Gorges Project. Notably, the Madao Hub set a new world record for daily concrete placement among similar projects, reaching a peak of 16 409 m 3  in a single day. These figures demonstrate that the construction intensity of the Pinglu Canal is exceptionally high compared with that of comparable large-scale projects. To sustain such a rapid construction pace, substantial labor and equipment resources are required. For instance, at the Madao Hub, 13 placement zones operate simultaneously, supported by 185 transport vehicles running continuously, 26 concrete-distribution equipment working collaboratively, and approximately 2 900 construction workers on site. Furthermore, the accelerated construction schedule results in high-frequency placement of mass concrete, shortened intervals between successive pours, and increased heat accumulation within the structure. Consequently, more intensive cooling-water circulation is required, leading to higher energy consumption and additional carbon emissions associated with temperature-control measures. In addition, rapid construction places greater demands on the early-age strength development of concrete, which limits the extensive use of low-carbon supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), such as fly ash and ground granulated blast-furnace slag, due to their relatively slower strength gain. Balancing “construction speed” and “low-carbon” under extreme schedule constraints has therefore become a critical challenge.

sections.heading: Restricted working space
paragraphs: Hydraulic hub projects along the canal are often located in constrained areas such as river confluences and narrow valleys, where surrounding mountains, waterways, farmland, and villages create narrow construction sites with severely limited space for lateral expansion and site layout (Fig.  2 ). This not only restricts logistics and on-site material handling but also limits the space available for material processing and storage. Moreover, the restricted working space intensifies interference among construction equipment, resulting in longer waiting and idle periods. Limited lifting and transportation routes often require detours and restrict equipment movement. The inability to deploy large, high-efficiency equipment frequently necessitates the use of multiple smaller machines, which reduces overall construction efficiency and increases energy consumption and associated carbon emissions. For example, at the Madao Hub, approximately 80 units of construction equipment including tower cranes, crawler cranes, and concrete placers must operate alongside more than 2 900 workers within an area of only 0.12 km 2 , covering approximately 120 concrete placement sections. Fig. 2 Working space of hub projects.  a  Madao.  b  Qishi.  c  Qingnian

Meanwhile, most hub structures of the Pinglu Canal are constructed using low-slump, three-graded concrete. The presence of large-sized coarse aggregates makes the workability of concrete difficult to control; consequently, the concrete is transported primarily by conveyor belts rather than by pumping. Therefore, to ensure effective transportation and subsequent vibratory compaction, high-density construction equipments must be arranged within the confined workspace. Improper management of restricted working space can lead to a sharp decline in construction efficiency, resulting in inefficient operation of machinery and increased energy consumption. It can also reduce the turnover efficiency of materials, requiring multiple handling and re-transportation, thereby increasing transportation-related energy consumption and ultimately elevating construction-related carbon emissions.

sections.heading: Summary: systemic challenges in safety and low-carbon synergy
paragraphs: The above five major technical challenges of the Pinglu Canal concrete works are not isolated issues but are interconnected, with carbon emissions serving as the linking factor. The inherent characteristics of this long, linear project and the mass-concrete requirements for the water-saving ship locks contribute to a high carbon footprint, primarily due to the massive consumption of materials and the long-haul transportation involved. The challenges associated with rapid construction and restricted working space further increase carbon intensity, since maintaining a high-speed and high-paced construction within limited working space significantly raises carbon emissions compared with conventional projects. Meanwhile, the requirements for long-term durability and rapid construction create a carbon trade-off over time: the project needs to be completed efficiently within a short schedule while ensuring a century-long service life. This requires balancing short-term construction emissions against long-term carbon costs associated with operation and maintenance.

Together, these challenges create a severe, systemic low-carbon dilemma for the Pinglu Canal. Based on current estimations, the carbon emissions from the Pinglu Canal concrete works are expected to exceed 4 Mt CO 2 e during the construction period from 2023 to 2026. The peak occurs during the intensive construction stages in 2024–2025, with annual emissions exceeding 1.5 Mt CO 2 e. The primary sources of carbon emissions come from the production of concrete and reinforcement steel, as well as fuel and electricity consumption. Therefore, it is essential to advance low-carbon construction while ensuring safety, durability, and reliability—achieving a synergy between safety and low-carbon goals. This is not only a critical response to global climate change, but also an inevitable trend toward unified control of carbon and cost throughout the project life cycle.

sections.heading: Solution strategy
paragraphs: Based on the aforementioned challenges, a solution strategic framework is proposed to achieve synergy between safety and low-carbon objectives for the Pinglu Canal concrete works. Measures must be taken across multiple project phases—from design and construction to operation and maintenance —and across multiple levels, including materials, structures, and the overall engineering system, to improve the low-carbon performance of concrete works while ensuring safety and reliability (Fig.  3 ). Fig. 3 Solution strategy

The design objective is to ensure that the calculated probability satisfies a prescribed target value, thereby integrating structural safety requirements with quantified carbon-emission constraints within a unified probabilistic framework. The target low-carbon conditional probability can be determined as the larger of two values: the acceptable value, derived from the carbon mitigation requirements of the construction sector, and the optimal value, obtained by minimizing carbon-related costs, following the methodology proposed by Xia et al. [ 9 ]. For the Pinglu Canal project, this probability threshold provides quantitative guidance for engineering design decisions, including the selection of low-carbon materials (e.g., recycled aggregates and fly ash replacement ratios), structural configuration (e.g., cross-sectional dimensions that influence embodied carbon emissions), and durability design (e.g., the target service life, which affects life-cycle carbon allocation and the allowable environmental impact), following the methodology proposed by Xia et al. [ 9 ,  10 ].

The carbon emission accounting in Eq. ( 1 ) adopts a cradle-to-construction-site system boundary, covering raw material extraction, material production, transportation, and on-site construction. For recycled materials (e.g., fly ash and recycled coarse aggregates produced from demolished bridge structures), a closed-loop LCA approach is adopted, in which the energy consumption associated with crushing and processing is explicitly included in the carbon emission inventory. Carbon emission factors are obtained from Chinese national standards and regional databases. The detailed LCA framework, system boundary, inventory analysis, and emission factor database, including the treatment of recycled aggregate processing, are presented by Xia et al. [ 11 ].

Furthermore, in the design stage, concrete reduction and optimization design should be carried out. Under the premise of fully ensuring structural safety and functional performance, scientific design methods should be applied to minimize the total consumption of cement and concrete throughout the canal project. Additionally, an ultra-high durability design needs to be implemented to ensure a service life exceeding 100 years, thereby minimizing the need for maintenance throughout the project life cycle.

In the construction stage, first, intelligent control of the time-varying properties of concrete should be implemented. This involves real-time monitoring, analysis, and regulation of the performance evolution of conventional or low-carbon concrete, thereby ensuring precise control of material properties. Second, human–machine collaboration in construction equipment needs to be achieved. Close coordination among various construction equipment and personnel across the concrete production and placement workflow—from raw material preparation to transportation and placement—can ensure the efficient execution of construction tasks. Third, full-domain digital–intelligent coordination should be established by integrating technologies such as the Internet of Things, digital twins, and artificial intelligence. This integration can create an intelligent collaboration system that covers all spatial domains, processes, and elements of concrete engineering, supporting smart scheduling and dynamic optimization toward low-carbon and high-efficiency construction.

In the operation and maintenance phase, an integrated aerial–aquatic–ground-based intelligent monitoring system for the canal structures should be established. By integrating various monitoring technologies across aerial, aquatic, and ground domains, a multidimensional smart monitoring network can be formed to continuously assess concrete structures. A multi-source data fusion method for concrete risk identification should also be developed, which involves feature extraction and integrated analysis using fusion algorithms on heterogeneous multi-source data, thereby enabling deep data mining for real-time identification and early warning of potential risks. Finally, an intelligent operation and maintenance decision-making system needs to be developed. Based on the identified potential risks, the system can predict degradation trends and shift maintenance strategies from passive repair to proactive prevention. It can thereby determine the optimal maintenance timing and strategies, thereby achieving efficient and low-carbon intelligent management.

At the material level, solid waste generated by canal construction and excavated earth resources should be utilized as sources of aggregates. Waste concrete can be crushed to prepare recycled aggregate concrete (RCA). Meanwhile, higher-quality excavated materials can be processed on-site and used as concrete aggregates, while lower-grade materials can be used in non-load-bearing structures such as eco-concrete and slope protection, thereby reducing carbon emissions from aggregate mining and transportation. Furthermore, since cement is the primary source of carbon emissions in construction. The use of low-carbon cementitious materials (CMs) including green cement and industrial solid waste-based SCMs derived from the canal can also significantly reduce cement consumption and carbon emissions. In addition, adopting high-performance concrete materials—such as ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) [ 12 ], engineered cementitious composites (ECC) [ 13 ], and fiber-reinforced concrete (FRC) [ 14 ]—can greatly enhance durability and extend the service life of concrete structures, thereby reducing maintenance frequency, life-cycle costs, and overall carbon emissions.

At the structural level, solid waste-based low-carbon concrete can be combined with conventional concrete to form composite mass-concrete structures. According to the stress characteristics and durability requirements of different zones, various types of concrete can be strategically arranged. For example, the use of low-carbon concrete made from solid waste in internal or low-stress areas, combined with conventional concrete or UHPC in external layers and critical load-bearing regions, would significantly increase the use of low-carbon concrete while ensuring structural safety. Furthermore, facilities such as temporary bridges, new bridges, service area buildings, waterway structures, and concrete components for slope protection works can be designed for disassembly and reuse. Such an approach enables easier component replacement during operation and maintenance, as well as recycling at the end of their service life. According to relevant studies, component reuse can offset up to 88% of carbon emissions [ 15 ], offering environmental and economic benefits throughout the project life cycle.

At the engineering-system level, intelligent technologies such as Building Information Modeling (BIM), big data, and digital twins should be applied to enable system integration. By comprehensively integrating information from all aspects of the canal project, a coordinated evaluation of safety performance and carbon emissions can be conducted, enabling multi-objective optimization and intelligent decision-making across the entire life cycle, including the design, construction, operation, maintenance, and even demolition phases. By considering all processes and factors, the safety and low-carbon performance of the concrete engineering can be significantly enhanced.

sections.heading: Recycled concrete
paragraphs: The construction of the Pinglu Canal involves not only the main lock structures but also the demolition and reconstruction of existing bridges along the route, as well as the construction of temporary works and permanent auxiliary facilities required for project implementation. If the large volume of waste concrete generated from bridge demolition can be recycled and reused on-site, the need for off-site waste disposal and natural aggregate extraction can be significantly reduced. This approach can effectively reduce carbon emissions associated with material production and transportation, while providing substantial environmental and economic benefits. Accordingly, a series of systematic recycling and reuse practices have been implemented during the construction of the Pinglu Canal.

Specifically, the Pinglu Canal project utilized demolition waste from the bridges along the canal route to produce recycled aggregates. Two mobile, modular production lines have been established, each consisting of concrete-crushing equipment, aggregate-shaping equipment, grading-screening devices, dust-removal systems, and loading machinery (Fig.  4 ). The produced recycled aggregates were applied in multiple components and diverse scenarios, including the construction of temporary bridges, buildings in the waterway management area, retaining walls, prefabricated slope protection, and mold-bag concrete revetments. The efficient reuse of demolished concrete contributes to the sustainable management of construction waste. Fig. 4 Modular recycled aggregates production lines.  a  Crushing equipment.  b  Grading and screening devices.  c  Shaping equipment

The temporary access bridge for the Shajing Qinjiang Bridge has a total length of 526 m and a width of 20 m. Recycled aggregates were used to prepare C50 recycled concrete for the bridge deck panels (Fig.  5 ). The slump of the recycled concrete was consistently maintained at 200 ± 10 mm, and its 28-day compressive strength reached 65.7 MPa. No cracks were observed since construction [ 16 ], and the bridge was officially opened to traffic in 2024. Furthermore, in Bridge Section 11, C40 concrete with 100% recycled coarse aggregate was used for the cap beams and pier columns (Fig.  6 ). The measured 7-day compressive strength reached 43.8 MPa, and the 28-day strength reached 52.6 MPa. Evidently, concrete using high-quality recycled aggregates derived from bridge demolition waste features a dense microstructure, enhanced crack resistance, and good workability, making it suitable for application in bridge structures. Fig. 5 Temporary access bridge for the Shajing Qinjiang Bridge.  a  Bridge deck construction.  b  Opened to traffic Fig. 6 100% recycled coarse aggregate concrete for Bridge Sect. 11.  a  Cap beams.  b  Pier columns

The multi-story permanent auxiliary buildings in the canal management areas are situated close to the canal construction sites, providing an ideal opportunity for the large-scale local recycling and utilization of construction and demolition waste. Recycled concrete with strengths ranging from C30 to C40 has been used in the construction of multi-story buildings, including the Qingnian Hub waterway management building and the Qinzhou comprehensive biodiversity monitoring station (Fig.  7 ). The application covered key structural components including beams, slabs, columns, and stairs, with a recycled aggregate replacement rate of 50%. The total volume of recycled concrete used amounted to 1 868 m 3 , with approximately 934 tonnes of recycled coarse aggregates utilized. Multiple tests were conducted to characterize the recycled aggregates and verify the recycled concrete mix ratio. The results confirmed that both the aggregate quality and concrete performance met the construction requirements. Fig. 7 Multi-story buildings using recycled concrete.  a  Qingnian Hub waterway management building.  b  Qinzhou comprehensive biodiversity monitoring station

Furthermore, 100% recycled coarse aggregate concrete was used in the construction of prefabricated slope protection, retaining walls, and mold-bag concrete revetments in waterway engineering. Additionally, low-grade stones excavated from earthworks were used to construct eco-concrete slopes (Fig.  8 ). Fig. 8 Application of solid waste-based recycled concrete in waterway engineering.  a  Prefabricated slope protection.  b  Retaining walls.  c  Mold-bag concrete revetments.  d  Eco-concrete slopes

Overall, the multi-scenario application of solid waste-based recycled concrete enabled the reuse of a large volume of construction waste, reduced the extraction of natural aggregates, and avoided long-distance transportation of aggregates, thereby delivering marked economic and carbon reduction benefits.

sections.heading: Optimization of mass concrete construction for water-saving ship locks
paragraphs: As previously mentioned, the application of mass concrete in the water-saving ship locks of the Pinglu Canal presents significant challenges to both construction and low-carbon requirements. To address these challenges, a three-graded concrete mix was adopted for most of the concrete used in the hub structures at the mix design stage. By optimizing the aggregate gradation, the demand for CMs was reduced. Since CMs are the main source of carbon emissions, this approach effectively reduces the overall carbon emissions.

At the mixing stage, the project established the largest intelligent concrete mixing plant in Asia, covering an area of over 70 000 m 2 . Through digital technologies, this plant enables intelligent optimization of concrete mix designs and precise batching. Additionally, comprehensive pre-cooling measures, including flake ice cooling, water cooling, and air cooling, were applied to control the concrete temperature at discharge, reducing the time required to achieve the design target of 16 ℃ by approximately 30%. The technology implemented at the Madao Hub concrete mixing plant improved the overall production efficiency by more than 30% and reduced the carbon emissions by more than 10%.

At the transportation stage specialized concrete transport trucks were developed for three-graded mass concrete by adjusting the power systems and mixing blade layout. These modifications reduced the vibration and segregation of the concrete during transport, ensuring the homogeneity of the three-graded concrete. Concurrently, an automatic vehicle identification and control system was installed on the transport trucks, enabling real-time vehicle tracking, route planning, and designated lanes assignment, thereby enhancing overall transportation efficiency.

At the casting stage, cantilever formwork was used for the sidewalls of the complex water-conveyance culverts, while custom-shaped steel forms were applied to the curved and chamfered sections. These techniques, combined with BIM modeling-assisted design, achieved the goal of tight fitting and seamless connections. To address the challenge of restricted working space, efficient multi-equipment combined concrete placement processes have been developed, including the “crawler-type distributor + mixer truck” method, “tower crane + lifting hopper + dump truck” method, and “shuttle-type distributor + dump truck” method [ 17 ]. This multi-equipment approach improved the placement efficiency by 2 to 3 times compared to conventional placement methods. Furthermore, equipment such as suspended group vibrators, crawler-type vibrating vehicles, and full-rotation folding arm vibrators was used to ensure efficient compaction of three-graded concrete with large aggregates (Fig.  9 ). An intelligent temperature control system for the mass concrete was also employed. The system continuously monitored the internal temperature field of the concrete and automatically adjusted the water valve based on cooling requirements, enabling intelligent temperature control [ 18 ]. This system maintained the temperature difference between the internal and external of the concrete below 20 ℃, ensuring the high-quality casting of mass concrete. Fig. 9 Placement and vibration equipment.  a  Crawler-type distributor.  b  Suspended group vibrators.  c  Crawler-type vibrating vehicles.  d  Full-rotation folding arm vibrators

Through the multi-stage optimization of mass concrete construction for the water-saving ship locks, refined management has been implemented throughout the entire process. As a result, this strategy has significantly improved the overall efficiency, and has achieved notable reductions in carbon emissions.

sections.heading: High-durability concrete for the canal
paragraphs: To ensure a service life of more than 100 years for the Pinglu Canal, extremely high requirements are imposed on concrete durability. To resist the potential chloride ion corrosion caused by saltwater intrusion, a “medium-heat cement + fly ash + slag powder” admixtures system is adopted, and the corrosion inhibitors are added to block the chloride ion penetration paths at the microscopic level. Meanwhile, a composite concrete material design strategy is adopted. A 2-m-thick layer of erosion-resistant concrete is used in the outer zone, while conventional concrete is used in the inner zone [ 19 ]. Through this differentiated material design approach with precise functional matching, structural durability is ensured while the overall carbon emissions of the concrete system are reduced. On the other hand, large saline collection pits are established combined with bubble curtain technology, based on the hydrological characteristics. Through active interception, this measure effectively suppresses the impacts of saltwater, reducing the intrusion rates by more than 50%. Together, the combination of material protection with engineering control measures provides a dual defense against chloride corrosion and effectively reduces the risk of rebar corrosion.

To address the erosion and abrasion caused by high-speed water flow in critical areas, such as the water conveyance culverts, the project applied an abrasion-resistant concrete mixture within 1 m of the culverts [ 20 ]. This mixture includes polyacrylonitrile fibers and silica powder. The toughening and cracking resistance of fibers, along with pore-filling effects of the silica power, significantly enhance the crack resistance, impact resistance, and abrasion resistance of the concrete. The concrete mix proportions for typical sections components are shown in Table  1 .
 Table 1 Concrete mix proportions for typical sections of the Pinglu Canal Unit: kg/m 3 Section Cement Fly ash Slag powder Silica fume Chloride ion penetration resistance enhancer Fiber Sand Coarse aggregate Water reducer Water 5–20 mm 20–40 mm 40–80 mm Qingnian hub – external concrete 141 56 56 0 28 0 685 417 417 556 3.90 104 Qingnian hub – internal concrete 141 70 70 0 0 0 685 417 417 556 3.90 104 Qishi hub– concrete around the culvert 219 100 0 13 0 1 826 574 574 0 5.15 136

To ensure high-quality concrete curing, an intelligent spray curing system is also implemented. This system uses a network of temperature and humidity sensors to monitor the surface conditions of concrete in real time and automatically adjusts the spraying frequency and intensity. Combined curing approaches are adopted, including covering the vertical and top surfaces with polymer water-saving and moisturizing membranes and applying thermal insulation blankets and boards. These measures maintain an optimal hydration environment, reduce cracking, and ensure the long-term durability of the structure.

sections.heading: Optimized structural design
paragraphs: Most ship lock structures in the canal are mass-concrete gravity structures. By adopting a multi-opening structure concept, material-reduction optimization can be achieved while ensuring structural safety and durability. In the Pinglu Canal, this approach is implemented in the main navigation wall of the Madao hub. A standard structural segment measuring 18 m × 18 m × 19 m was optimized by incorporating multiple vertical openings within the concrete, while maintaining a 1-m solid perimeter zone to guarantee load-bearing capacity and durability (Fig.  10 a). Fig. 10 Optimized navigation wall.  a  Structural schematic.  b  Temperature control measures [ 21 ]

During construction, the openings were shaped using plastic corrugated pipes, with their upper ends open to the exterior at the top, allowing internal heat to dissipate through water injection or ventilation measures (Fig.  10 b). Upon completion, the openings were backfilled with sand and crushed stone, after which the top layer was cast.

Coupled thermal-force finite element simulations were conducted to analyze the temperature fields under different cooling measures, and the results were validated by on-site measurements [ 21 ]. The results showed that water injection achieved the best cooling performance, reducing the peak temperature by approximately 9.5 ℃, followed by air discharge and water cooling. The optimized design reduced concrete consumption and energy use for thermal control while achieving effective temperature management, thereby cutting construction costs by 240 000 yuan and carbon emissions by 35.8 tonnes [ 22 ], showing significant economic and environmental benefits.

sections.heading: Smart canal concrete construction
paragraphs: To enable smart construction, the Pinglu Canal construction management team has adopted information technologies such as the Beidou Navigation Satellite System, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence. A digital twin platform for the smart canal has been established, enabling intelligent management and control throughout the entire construction process.

In terms of schedule and quality management, over 4 400 sensing devices have been installed on numerous pieces of large-scale machinery and critical structures. These include stress- and strain- monitoring, temperature, displacement and settlement, video-monitoring, and equipment-positioning sensors, with the collected data transmitted via wired fiber optic networks and 5G technology. The data collected from these devices are synchronized to the digital twin platform. Utilizing big-data analytics and machine-learning algorithms, the platform cleans, integrates, and updates the collected data, ensuring the digital twin model remains synchronized with the physical system and achieving real-time monitoring of the construction process. For example, during concrete placement of the Qingnian Hub ship lock, temperature monitoring was implemented for each concrete block. Ambient-air and concrete-surface temperature sensors were installed, and three monitoring sections were arranged at different positions along the central vertical axis of the mass concrete to continuously capture its internal temperature evolution. The monitored data were transmitted in real time to the digital twin platform, where the temperature difference between the concrete interior and surface was calculated and subsequent temperature development was predicted. When the platform predicted that the difference between the peak internal temperature and the surface temperature would exceed the 20 ℃ threshold, the system automatically issued an alarm and performed inverse analysis to determine the optimal cooling water temperature and flow rate, thereby supporting timely adjustments to the temperature-control measures. Furthermore, by integrating the BIM model with actual three-dimensional (3D) renderings, the construction progress status of concrete components is visually represented by different colors. Clicking on any component allows access to its information on pouring records, temperature control data, and quality acceptance (Fig.  11 a). Fig. 11 Digital twin platform.  a  Smart management.  b  UAVs system.  c  Large language model assistant

In terms of safety assurance, the digital twin platform employs cameras deployed along the construction route and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to automatically detect whether workers are wearing safety helmets and reflective vests. Violations will be immediately flagged, and audible alerts will be issued. The UAVs system integrates multi-modal sensing terminals and algorithms to enable intelligent, all-scenario inspections (Fig.  11 b). Operating both day and night, the system can reach any designated task point within a 5 km radius in less than five minutes.

Concurrently, the Pinglu Canal has completed the local deployment of the DeepSeek large language model and integrated it with the digital twin platform (Fig.  11 c). The large language model is directly connected to the digital twin database and can access project-wide data on construction, equipment operation, material consumption, carbon-emissions, and safety monitoring. Based on in-depth correlation analysis of massive engineering datasets, the model automatically generates multidimensional visualization reports, identifies risk patterns, evaluates the effectiveness of carbon-reduction measures, such as the utilization of green electricity and the recyling of excavation-material, and provides optimized low-carbon construction strategies and resource-allocation plans. According to project statistics, the digital twin platform saves approximately 4 240 tonnes of fuel, 1.6 million kWh of electricity, and 8 000 tonnes of cement annually, corresponding to a reduction of about 280 000 t CO 2  in carbon emissions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and prospects
paragraphs: The concrete engineering of the Pinglu Canal faces stringent requirements for safety, durability, and reliability, alongside significant pressure to reduce carbon emissions. This paper systematically examines the specific challenges encountered in canal’s concrete works, including the project’s long, linear layout, mass concrete for water-saving ship locks, long-term durability requirements, rapid construction, and restricted working space. We further analyze the associated systemic low-carbon challenges, highlighting the need to enhance the low-carbon performance of construction while ensuring structural safety and long-term durability, thereby achieving safety-low-carbon synergy. In response to these challenges, a multi-stage and multi-level solution framework is proposed, centered on the “safety-low-carbon synergy” across design, construction, and operation and maintenance phases, as well as the material, structural, and project system levels. Demonstration applications within the Pinglu Canal project are presented, showing that the implemented technologies can effectively reduce life-cycle carbon footprint while improving engineering quality and construction efficiency.

Although some low-carbon techniques have already been applied in the Pinglu Canal concrete works, research on low-carbon construction for canal concrete remains at an early stage. The following low-carbon concrete technologies show considerable potential for further research and applications:
Recycled concrete-block-filled concrete technology

Block-filled concrete is a specialized construction method for mass-concrete structures. Large stone blocks are first placed into the formwork, after which highly flowable concrete is poured to fill the voids, and the whole mass finally hardens into an integral concrete structure. For mass-concrete structures of canals, waste concrete can be crushed and processed into large precast recycled concrete blocks. A layered construction can then be adopted: the bottom layer concrete is poured first, followed by the lifting and placement of the precast blocks and the subsequent pouring of concrete for that layer. This process is repeated until the entire structure is completed. The precast blocks can incorporate reinforcing ribs on surfaces and cavities inside to enhance mechanical interlocking. While the precast blocks may lead to a slight increase in cost, this technology not only enables efficient utilization of solid waste but also significantly reduces cement consumption, lowers the hydration heat, and decreases overall the carbon emissions. However, several challenges remain before its widespread application in canal engineering. Further research is required on the long-term bond performance between recycled concrete blocks and cast-in-place concrete, the durability of the composite structure under complex canal environments, and optimized design methods for block size and placement ratio.
High-toughness concrete technology

The toughness of concrete refers to its ability to absorb energy and resist crack propagation while deformation under loading. During seismic events, structural components made of high-toughness concrete can dissipate seismic energy through inelastic deformation, thereby reducing the risk of sudden collapse. Such materials also exhibit enhanced resistance to extreme impact loads, including explosions and vessel collisions, and possess post-disaster recovery ability, enabling the rapid restoration of load-bearing capacity and serviceability through appropriate repair measures. Although adopting high-toughness concrete increases initial construction costs, this additional investment is negligible compared with the potential economic losses associated with navigation interruptions caused by maintenance or structural damage. For example, the blockage of the Suez Canal in 2021 lasted six days, resulting in transit fee losses of approximately USD 15 million per day and an estimated global economic loss of USD 136.9 billion [ 23 ]. The life-cycle benefits of high-toughness concrete have also been demonstrated in studies on ECC pavements. Owing to their extended service life and reduced maintenance requirements, ECC pavements achieved a 63.2%–68.5% reduction in life-cycle carbon emissions, while their life-cycle cost was only 9.60%–23.3% of those of conventional pavements [ 24 ]. Therefore, high-toughness concrete has considerable potential to reduce both life-cycle carbon emissions and maintenance-related economic losses in canal infrastructure. However, the long-term durability and toughness retention of high-toughness concrete under the coupled effects of water immersion, chloride penetration, wetting–drying cycles, and mechanical loading remain insufficiently understood, particularly for canal structures with service lives exceeding 100 years.
Carbon accounting database and emission factors for canal construction

Construction-phase carbon accounting for canal projects is still at an early stage, and comprehensive carbon emission databases and localized emission factors for canal construction are currently lacking [ 25 ]. Future research should establish standardized carbon accounting methods covering the entire construction process and develop carbon emission databases for key construction activities, materials, equipment, and transportation modes. Particular attention should be given on establishing localized carbon emission factors for typical canal construction processes and materials. These efforts will provide a reliable basis for life-cycle carbon assessment, low-carbon design optimization, and carbon-performance benchmarking among future canal projects.
